There is no "the" in the lyrics. The lyrics are "that's a problem with a closed door."  Not that's the problem with a closed door. "The" changes the context of the lyric. What he's saying by the verse "that's a problem with a closed door" is he doesn't care that people don't talk about him too much no more. It's in reference to being interviewed and often interviewers will say things like that to try and get artist to give up info on future projects. So, if an interviewer says, "I hear they don't talk about you too much no more." The hope is.... it strikes the ego, a bait statement and gets an artist to be like. Yo I'm still john blaze like that. I'm working on this and this and I got this coming, but really the artist might just be in a spell of depression, burnt out, tired. But no one wants to hear that, they just want the good news.  If you don't add or change the lyrics you 'll get a more accurate picture of what the artist is trying to paint.

This song is devastating, if you were to separate the instrumental and the lyrics and examine them separately they completely contrast each other. The melody is calming, peacefully progresses, and would sound like something that would make someone happy. Then you read the lyrics, and it reads as someone who has completely given up on life and this world entirely. Yet the lyrics and the instrumental pair so perfectly. I couldn't imagine any other instrumental expressing the lyrics any better. In a way, it makes sense. When you truly give up, the weight of shame, sadness, anger, and torturous confusion for failing and being looked down upon so many times fades. Now you are left with nothing but you and what ever it is you feel in the present moment now that you have let go of everything. For most, I would assume they would feel nothing, but for Mac, I would like to imagine he felt at peace in his final moments, just like the way the song feels. R.I.P Mac Miller, and thank you for creating the masterpiece that is "Good News".
